## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll read the last two reviews, choose 20k, and play game 143 to completion. I’ll check eye space at the first cap and save the full game with a review for the next session.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

Played 2026-10-07. 9×9 Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko.
Black51/White52 consecutive passes ended the game; board() confirms W+42, next53.

Read142/141 and30 before play. Selected20k on the empty Black board before C3.
All52 actual moves replay legally and match all28 raw boards, capture totals, next numbers and ko markers.

${l.moves.map(m=>m.n+' '+m.color+' '+m.move).join(', ')}.

## Opening: both side junctions became contested

C3/G7 established diagonal bases. C5 extended left; White D3 approached C3.
C4 actually joined C3/C5, preventing that cutting gap.
G5 extended the right boundary, but remained separate from G7.
Before11 the manual OPEN target was ABC all nine rows27 +GHJ rows5–9 fifteen =42.
Black needs45 with every point assigned and komi7, so even this intact aspiration was insufficient.

White12 G6 occupied the right junction. G5 then had only F5/H5.
H5/H6 extended around that cut; White D6 approached the other open junction C6.
Black17 H7 actually joined G7 to H6/H5/G5.
White18 C6 joined D6, splitting the left.
This is the concrete two-junction problem: broad jumps on both sides left more repair obligations than could be handled in one turn.
It does not establish C7 or H7 as individually inferior to a particular alternative.
Future experiments need a connection plan against the opponent occupying the shared point, not just a broad coordinate target.

B6 began separate with A6/B5/B7.
White D7 left C7 only B7/C8; B7 actually joined B6/C7.
B5 later joined that upper chain to C5/C4/C3, routing around White C6.

White24 C8 capped upper-left expansion. B8 joined B7, then B9 secured the first-line endpoint.
White D8 joined C8 to D7/D6, and White C9 joined that chain.
Black did not chase those White stones or claim their liberties as territory.

White26 C2 approached the lower endpoint.
B3 joined C3, B2 joined B3 after further play, and B1 secured the first line.
White D2 actually joined C2 to D3/D4; White C1 joined the same chain.
No atari capture or recapture supplied life.

A5 joined B5 and divided left upper A6–A9 four-point space from the lower region.
D5 joined C5 and gained one mixed boundary point; it captured nothing.
A3 joined B3 and split the lower region into:
- A1/A2, bounded by B1/B2/A3;
- A4/B4, bounded by A3/A5/B3/B5/C4.

Every boundary stone belongs to one connected fifteen-stone Black chain.
These are independent true two-point eye rooms. Entry into either can be captured at its other point while the other room remains.
The upper four-point edge room supplies additional space; it is one room, not four eyes.
The fifteen left stones survive and score23:15 stones+8 empties.
B1/B9 retained endpoints, A5/A3 divided eyes, and D5 supplied the only final outside gain.
Internal life moves did not add area under Chinese scoring.

## Right: a completed divider did not protect its lower room

G8/G9 joined and retained the upper endpoint against F8/F9.
H8 joined G8/H7. White36 J5 then began at J4/J6.
Black37 J8 joined H8 and completed the upper edge divider.
H9/J9 is one independent true two-point eye region.
The other putative region J6/J7 remained enemy-bordered by J5.

White38 J6 joined J5 and invaded that lower space, retaining J4/J7.
This is the key failure: obtaining one true room does not prove life if the second room is accessible from an outside enemy chain.
At J5, reading only the planned J8 divider omitted the immediate J6 continuation.
A different earlier boundary/divider plan is an experiment, not a proved superior move or forced winning line.

Black39 F7 joined G7 and temporarily added E7.
White40 E7 joined D7 and removed that new liberty.
Right ten then had F5/H9/J7/J9.
White42 F5 joined E5/F4/F6 and joined G6 through F6, removing F5.
Right ten now had H9/J7/J9.
White48 J4 actually joined J5/J6 to H4/main.
White50 J7 extended that chain; right ten ended with only H9/J9.
No adjacent White chain was in atari.
F7 expanded the stone chain but produced no eye or surviving area.

Final right ten: F7/G5/G7/G8/G9/H5/H6/H7/H8/J8.
Their two liberties H9/J9 are adjacent: ONE eye region, not two eyes and not seki.

Manual terminal example, UNPLAYED:
White H9 entry has sole J9, with Black still retaining J9.
Black J9 captures that entry and reopens H9; all eleven Black stones now have sole H9.
White H9 legally captures all eleven. No simple ko: the recapture removes eleven stones.
If Black fills H9 first, White J9 directly captures eleven; filling J9 first similarly allows White H9.
Other Black moves cannot restore the closed room or capture a neighboring White chain in one turn.

left27 loses C6/C8/C9/C2/C1 five, gains D5 one =>23;
right15 loses G6/J5/J6/J7 four, gains F7 one =>12.

Final Black23=42−five+one−twelve−three? This expression would mix reference stages and is NOT used.
Use the disjoint ledger: (27−5+1)+(15−4+1−12)=23+0=23.

neutral0. This would imply W+18 if all stones lived, but the right ten do not live.

former right12, and lower-central seventeen.

Do not count a one-eye group's stones or territory as safe merely because the display assigns every point.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
